Newborn Care

Umbilical granuloma in a newborn: diagnosis and treatment

Updated: November 14, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A small moist lump can remain in the centre of the navel after a baby's cord stump comes away. It may leave a pale stain on the diaper each time the surface rubs against it. One possible cause is an umbilical granuloma, a small patch of healing tissue. Arrange for a clinician to look at a lump that persists or keeps draining. Seek urgent care sooner if redness spreads onto the abdomen, the area becomes tender or the baby seems unwell.

Why the last patch of tissue can stay moist

As the cord base heals, new tissue grows over the area. Sometimes a soft piece of this tissue remains exposed after the rest of the navel has begun to dry. A granuloma may look pink, red or brownish and can release a little clear or light-yellow fluid. The timing is a clue. A clinician expects to see the lump after the cord separates and checks that the skin around it looks healthy.

A confirmed granuloma is benign and generally causes little discomfort. A baby who cries when the surrounding skin is touched, develops thick or foul-smelling drainage, or starts feeding poorly needs a different assessment. The exact reason one baby's navel develops a granuloma while another heals without one is often uncertain. Its appearance does not mean a parent failed to wash or dry the cord correctly.

What the clinician looks for at the visit

The clinician will ask when the cord separated, when you first saw the lump, whether it has changed and what has collected on the diaper. Mention if the area stays wet continuously even after you gently dry it, whether the skin seems sore, and any treatment already put on it. The examination includes the base and surface of the lump, the surrounding abdominal skin and how the baby is doing overall.

A typical small granuloma in an otherwise well infant can often be identified on examination. A photograph can document a change between visits, but it cannot show exactly where fluid is coming from or distinguish every red nodule. If the lump is unusually firm, looks like an opening or has not responded to appropriate treatment, ask whether another cause should be considered before anyone cauterizes it again.

When drainage or a bulge suggests something different

Fluid that looks or smells like urine can occasionally come through a connection to the bladder that remained open before birth. A connection to the intestine can allow bowel contents to drain at the navel. A small umbilical polyp, made of tissue left behind during development, can resemble a granuloma. These findings call for prompt medical assessment and may need a pediatric surgeon. Do not probe the opening, squeeze the lump or try to identify the fluid by testing it at home.

A soft bulge covered by ordinary skin that pushes outward during crying has a different appearance. An umbilical hernia is an opening in the abdominal wall and is assessed separately from a moist surface nodule. Many hernias close as a child grows through the preschool years. A fixed deadline in the second year cannot predict an individual child's course. Ask the clinician to explain which finding they see and what changes would matter for that diagnosis.

Observation or treatment after confirmation

If the baby is well and the clinician is confident the lump is a small granuloma, observation for a short period can be reasonable. Ask how long to wait, whether the nodule should shrink and who will check it if the navel still leaves a wet mark. A clearly agreed review date is more helpful than assuming all lumps must vanish a particular number of days after birth.

Persistent moisture or a granuloma that continues to grow can lead to treatment aimed at drying and healing the exposed tissue. Treating a confirmed granuloma and treating an infection are different decisions. A baby with spreading inflammation needs urgent medical care regardless of whether a small area of granulation tissue is also present. A planned treatment appointment should never delay that assessment.

What happens with silver nitrate

Silver nitrate is a chemical a trained clinician can apply to the granuloma. It changes the treated tissue so it dries and shrinks. The surrounding skin needs to be protected because the same chemical can burn healthy skin. Ask how the team will keep the chemical on the target area and what appearance to expect afterward. The treated spot can darken, and staining can also appear nearby.

The procedure is usually brief. Granulation tissue can be relatively insensitive, but the adjacent skin can hurt or blister if it is injured. A change limited to the treated spot is different from expanding soreness, raw or peeling skin, or increasing redness. Contact the treating service about those changes. Do not purchase a cautery stick, repeat the procedure yourself or assume that crying or pain is an expected part of healing.

Salt and other options used by care teams

Some newborn services offer a clinician-directed course of common salt after confirming an uncomplicated granuloma. Others use silver nitrate first. Small clinical trials have studied salt as an alternative, but a small open-label study cannot establish that one method is best for every baby. Local plans differ. If your clinician recommends salt, obtain their instructions and review arrangements for your baby. A wet navel that has never been examined is a different situation.

For selected persistent lesions a specialist may consider another office procedure, such as freezing the tissue, or tying the base of a suitable stalk with a surgical ligature. Some lesions are excised and examined to clarify their identity. These methods have different indications and possible local injury. Never freeze, cut or tie tissue at home. In particular, treatment intended for a superficial granuloma will not close an abnormal connection to the bladder or bowel.

If the first treatment does not settle it

Ask what counts as improvement. The nodule should become smaller or drier, moisture should lessen and the surrounding skin should stay comfortable. Some babies need another clinician-applied treatment. Bring the baby back on the agreed date if the lump stays much the same, returns or continues to leak. The useful question at that visit is whether the original diagnosis still fits.

A persistent red nodule, especially with unusual drainage, can warrant specialist examination and sometimes imaging or removal for tissue diagnosis. A clinician may still find a straightforward granuloma. The value of reassessment is that it can also identify a polyp or tract that needs another approach. Repeating stronger chemicals or covering an opening with a tight dressing can obscure what the examiner needs to see.

Infection signs require a faster response

Seek urgent medical care now if redness spreads from the navel, red streaks run outward, there is swelling and tenderness, or foul pus appears with inflammation. Infection in this area is called omphalitis and can progress quickly in a newborn. A rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or above in a baby younger than three months requires immediate medical assessment. A newborn can also be seriously ill without a fever.

Poor feeding, marked irritability, unusual sleepiness, breathing difficulty or a baby who is hard to wake needs urgent help. Call emergency services for breathing difficulty or reduced responsiveness. Contact a clinician immediately for active bleeding that continues. If the navel is simply still damp and the baby is well, arrange examination of the lump. You do not need to wait two weeks to ask about a change that concerns you.

Day-to-day care while awaiting review

Keep the area clean and dry, fold the diaper edge away from the navel and avoid pulling on the tissue. A sponge wash can help keep an unhealed navel dry. Follow the treating service's instructions for bathing after a procedure. If the original cord stump is still attached after three weeks, arrange a medical review. A late-separating stump and a moist lump after separation are two distinct findings.

There is no established way for a family to prevent every granuloma. Skip attempts to speed drying with powders, alcohol, herbal products or tight coverings unless the newborn team has prescribed a specific care plan. Bring the sequence of changes to follow-up: when the cord came away, how the area looked before treatment, and what is different now. For routine healing and care after separation, see https://bemamas.com/newborn/care-after-the-umbilical-cord-falls-off/

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Have the baby examined to distinguish healing tissue from infection, a polyp, hernia or deeper tract.

If a clinician treats a granuloma, ask about skin protection, expected drying and the date for reassessment.

Escalate spreading redness, fever or signs of illness promptly, and request review for persistent or unusual drainage.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize the date of cord separation, descriptions of drainage and your follow-up plan. A newborn clinician can examine the lump, distinguish causes and choose treatment.

When to seek help

Get urgent assessment for spreading redness, tenderness, foul pus or an unwell newborn. A temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or above in a baby younger than three months needs immediate medical attention. Breathing difficulty or reduced responsiveness warrants emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: November 14, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A persistent moist nodule after cord separation should be examined so the cause of drainage is clear.
  • A little pale fluid can occur with a granuloma, while thick pus, spreading redness, tenderness or an unwell newborn needs urgent assessment.
  • Silver nitrate can help a granuloma dry and can burn normal skin. It belongs in trained hands.
  • Some services recommend salt after diagnosis. A lump that fails to improve deserves another examination before further treatment.
  • Urine-like or stool-like drainage is a reason for prompt medical review for a possible deeper connection.

Frequently asked questions

What does an umbilical granuloma look like?

It often appears as a small soft, moist spot in the middle of the navel after cord separation. It can be pink or red and leak a little pale fluid. Appearance alone cannot confirm the diagnosis. Seek assessment for persistent wetness, unusual discharge or redness extending onto the surrounding skin.

How long should it take for the cord and navel to dry?

The stump usually separates during the first few weeks. If it is still attached after three weeks, let the baby's clinician know. A navel may look unfinished briefly after separation, but a persisting wet nodule deserves review. Seek care sooner for active bleeding, infection signs or illness.

Can an umbilical granuloma hurt my baby?

A confirmed granuloma is a benign growth of healing tissue and is usually comfortable. Tender skin, spreading redness, foul discharge or fever are reasons for urgent reassessment. The surrounding skin can also be injured by chemicals used in treatment, so report soreness or blistering afterward.

How is a newborn's umbilical granuloma treated?

The clinician may advise brief observation or a treatment such as silver nitrate, with protection for the nearby skin. Some services recommend salt once the diagnosis is clear. Persistent lesions can need further review or a specialist procedure. Ask when the baby should return and which changes warrant an earlier call.

Does urine-like fluid need another silver nitrate treatment?

It needs medical examination first. Urine-like or stool-like drainage can indicate a connection to the bladder or bowel. Repeated cauterization of the surface cannot correct that problem and could postpone the care the baby needs.

Is a bulge that appears during crying another granuloma?

A skin-covered bulge that becomes more obvious with crying may be an umbilical hernia. A granuloma is a small moist surface growth. Have either finding assessed if you are uncertain. The follow-up and treatment decisions are different.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
